extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of public relations (PR students, PR professionals, communication researchers)
extracted.subtask_description: Chapter-level textbook guidance on understanding and measuring public opinion (orientation/coorientation) and on the goals, culture, and practices of internal relations/employee communication. Covers measurement criteria, coorientational constructs and consensus types, diagnostic problems for organization–public relationships, and conditions and channels for effective internal communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement sensitivity and depth in public opinion research
rubrics_metrics.description: Describing and understanding public opinion requires greater measurement sensitivity and depth than the simple yes–no questions often used in telephone polling; public opinion reflects a dynamic process of interpersonal and media communication among groups who can act similarly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter notes that typical binary polling is insufficient; recommends richer measures (see Chapters 11 and 12). Remember that “thinking together” often leads to “acting together,” so measurement should capture degrees of salience, pertinence, expressed opinion, and perceived social support. Treat informational and social support as giving predisposition weight/inertia (strongly supported opinions are resistant to change).

rubrics_metrics.name: Orientation — salience and pertinence
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual orientation comprises two sources of value for objects: salience (feelings derived from prior history and reinforcements) and pertinence (relative value found by object-by-object comparisons depending on attributes and context).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To describe and understand an individual's opinion about an object you must measure both salience (what the individual brings to the situation) and pertinence (how the individual defines the situation). This distinction clarifies attitude vs opinion relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attitudinal system components (evaluative frames, cognition, affection, conation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Attitude systems comprise four components: (1) evaluative frames of reference (values and interests), (2) cognition (knowledge and beliefs), (3) affection (feelings), and (4) conation (behavioral intentions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this broader nomenclature to avoid confusing the affective response mode with the entire attitude system. Attitudes are cross-situational predispositions informed by lifetime experience and information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between opinion and attitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Opinion is the judgment expressed about an object in a particular situation; attitudes are more basic, enduring predispositions to respond across situations. Opinions are generally verbal/overt and more situational and cognitive; attitudes are more affective, global, and enduring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only expressed opinions enter public opinion processes; unexpressed intrapersonal predispositions do not. When measuring public opinion, focus on expressed, situational judgments while recognizing their relation to underlying attitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coorientation (definition and scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: Coorientation exists when two or more individuals' orientations include the same issues/objects and include each other — i.e., they are oriented to something in common and to each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coorientational models link intrapersonal constructs (salience, pertinence) to interpersonal constructs (perceived agreement, accuracy, agreement, understanding). Effective PR uses coorientational measurement to assess both parties’ views and perceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coorientational construct — congruency / perceived agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Congruency (often called perceived agreement) describes the extent to which your own views match your estimate of another's views on the same issue; it is an intrapersonal construct used to formulate interaction strategies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perceived agreement influences chosen communication strategies; misjudging another’s position can lead to inappropriate responses until corrected by interaction. PR practitioners should measure perceived agreement to guide responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coorientational construct — accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Accuracy represents the extent to which your estimate of another's views matches that person's actual views; because it requires comparison of observations from two people, accuracy is an interpersonal construct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accuracy determines appropriateness of actions. Unlike perceived agreement, accuracy can be improved through communication; measuring accuracy is essential for diagnosing relationship problems and prescribing corrective actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coorientational construct — agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Agreement represents the extent to which two or more persons share similar evaluations of an issue of mutual interest; in individual-orientation terms, agreement compares saliences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agreement indicates actual similarity of evaluations; note that perceptions of agreement may differ from actual agreement and both matter for public behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coorientational construct — understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding measures the similarities in the definitions held by two or more persons; in individual-orientation terms, understanding compares pertinences (how each defines the situation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High understanding means parties define the issue similarly; PR communication should aim to increase shared definitions where needed rather than merely trying to change levels of agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of coorientational consensus (monolithic consensus, dissensus, false consensus, pluralistic ignorance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Four states of coorientational consensus: monolithic consensus (majority actually agrees and perceives majority agreement), dissensus (majority actually disagrees and perceives disagreement), false consensus (actual disagreement but majority perceives agreement), and pluralistic ignorance (majority actually agrees but perceives little agreement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish actual agreement from perceived agreement; inaccurate perceptions (false consensus, pluralistic ignorance) can be changed via communication and often drive public behavior more than actual agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization–public relationship problems (three diagnostic types)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three PR problems identifiable via coorientation: (1) the organization and a public hold different definitions of an issue (they are talking about different things); (2) the organization's perceptions of a public's views do not match the public's actual views (management acts on inaccurate estimates); (3) members of a public hold inaccurate perceptions of the organization's positions on an issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In all cases, relationship harm stems from differing definitions and inaccurate perceptions, not necessarily disagreement. Corrective communication should focus on creating shared definitions and increasing cross-perception accuracy (example: Army Corps of Engineers failed to communicate disadvantages, leading to costly delays). Sometimes simply reporting the public's actual views to management is the needed corrective action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coorientational measures as research, planning, and outcome criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Coorientational measures provide (1) information to identify and describe organization–public relationship problems, (2) guidance for planning appropriate messages/responses, and (3) outcome criteria (agreement, understanding, congruency, accuracy) to track how relationships change after communication and corrective actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated coorientational measurement indicates whether communication improved shared definitions and accuracy. Use measures to design atypical but efficient solutions (e.g., if management misperceives public views, deliver actual views to management rather than attempting to change public opinion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal relations goals and imperatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal relations (employee communication) is building and maintaining relationships with internal publics (employees at all levels); goals include timely, complete, and accurate corporate communication and fostering two-way communication and manager accountability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizations must treat employees as their most important public. PR should cultivate a manager communication network making every supervisor accountable for communicating effectively about key business and public issues (not just job-related information). Failure to prioritize two-way communication risks disengagement, absenteeism, poor quality, and reputational harm (example: Domino's employee video scandal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions characterizing effective working relationships (seven conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Seven ideal conditions for effective working relationships: (1) confidence and trust between employer and employees; (2) honest, candid information flowing up, down, and sideways; (3) satisfying status and participation for each person; (4) continuity of work without strife; (5) healthy or safe surroundings; (6) success for the enterprise; (7) optimism about the future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chief executive must establish and endorse this culture as formal policy. Even with top support, barriers to two-way communication remain; building these conditions mitigates ‘slothing on the job’ and other costs of poor internal communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Channels and means for encouraging two-way internal communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Face-to-face communication with an 'open-door policy' is the primary medium for encouraging upward, two-way communication and building good working relationships; internal relations employs both nonmediated and mediated means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opinion research shows fewer than half of employees rate organizations highly on downward (management-to-employee) or upward (employee-to-management) communication; prioritize face-to-face and manager networks to improve listening and information flow. Consider regulatory and business contexts when choosing mediated vs nonmediated channels.
